However, studies on the change in functional diversity across ecosystems are still scarce, especially for soil fauna (Salmon et al., 2014). Soil fauna plays a critical role within natural and agroecosystems (Marsden et al., 2020). Their role in organic matter decomposition, nutrient cycling, and the maintenance of soil structure (Menta and Remelli, 2020) is inherently linked to the health of the soil (Kibblewhite et al., 2008). As the taxonomic diversity of these taxa can be sensitive to changes in soil properties and micro-habitat characteristics (Fichaux et al., 2019), functional diversity is also expected to be sensitive to these changes (Fontanilla et al., 2019).

Dead wood cover was significantly higher within the indigenous forests and eucalypt compartments compared to the grasslands (Table S6). Leaf litter cover was significantly higher within the eucalypt compartments, followed by the indigenous forests and grasslands (Table S6). Soil compaction was significantly lower within the indigenous forests and grasslands compared to the eucalypt compartments (Table S6). Soil moisture was significantly lower within the grasslands and eucalypt compartments compared to the indigenous forests (Table S6). No significant difference in soil pH was found between the three habitat types (Table S6). Vegetation cover was significantly higher within the grasslands, followed by the indigenous forests and eucalypt compartments (Table S6).

[prose] We divided the traits for ants and springtails into three categories: 1) morphological traits, 2) feeding strategy, and 3) habitat position (i.e., microhabitat occurrence). For ants, traits used in the analysis (Table S2) were derived from the literature (eye size, habitat position and feeding strategy) (Table S3) or measured in the laboratory (body length, femur length and darkness of the integument). For springtails, body length was measured in the laboratory, and all other traits (eye size, furca development, feeding strategy and habitat position) (Table S4) were determined using previous work on springtails traits (see Salmon et al., 2014; Raymond-Léonard et al., 2019). This was verified by a taxonomic expert (CJS) and a family-level key to the Collembola of South Africa ([https://collembola.co.za/identification-keys/](https://collembola.co.za/identification-keys/)). [prose] springtails) and femur length (ants) were measured using a Leica MZ7s dissecting microscope (Leica Microsystems, Germany). Where possible, six individuals per species were measured, and an average body length (for both taxa), and femur length (for ants only) was estimated. For polymorphic ants, individuals of varying sizes were selected, and an average body length calculated for those species. The body length of each ant species was measured dorsally from the tip of the mandible to the tip of the gaster, whereas femur length was measured in anterior view as it is a good proxy for overall leg length (Queiroz et al., 2015), and only the hind femur was measured. Ant integument colour was examined by the same method proposed by Bishop et al. (2016), using HSV (hue, saturation, and value) estimates, extracted from photos of the specimens using the image editing software [paint.NET](http://paint.NET) (v.4.0.3). Hue describes the dominant wavelength, while saturation indicates the amount of hue present in the colour and the value sets the amount of light in the colour (Bishop et al., 2016). [prose] Using pitfall trapping, four 300 ml plastic cups (9.5 cm diameter and 8 cm deep) were placed in $\mathrm { ~ a ~ 2 ~ m ~ } ^ { 2 }$ grid at each site. The rim of the trap was level with the soil surface and filled with 50 ml of 60% ethylene glycol (containing a small amount of detergent to break the surface tension). Traps were left in the field for seven days, after which they were collected. Secondly, arthropods were collected directly using an aspirator within a randomly placed 1 m quadrat of each site. This was conducted for 10 min by two people. Arthropods were also extracted using the Tullgren-Berlese extraction technique from 1 L of collected soil from each site (10 × 100 ml subsamples randomly collected). The soil was placed on top of a 0.5 mm aperture size mesh and left for 7 days to allow soil to dry and arthropods to be extracted into the attached 75% ethanol jar below the funnel. Specimens collected from all sampling methods were sorted into morphospecies $( \mathbf { i . e . } ,$ using external morphological characteristics only, without the use of identification keys) (Oliver and Beattie, 1996) (from here on referred to as ‘species’) and counted. Springtail and ant specimens were identified by taxonomic experts (A. Ndaba – for ants, CJS – for springtails). Springtails were identified to family level and ants to genus level. These taxonomic levels were of sufficient resolution for obtaining certain traits from the literature that do not vary substantially within these taxonomic groupings (section 2.3. Functional traits).

Ant body size is also partly related to thermoregulation, as larger bodies enable organisms to lose heat slower than smaller bodied organisms, and larger organisms would be expected in cooler, canopied environments. This was observed in Zululand, with smaller individuals in grassland compared to the wooded biotopes. However, the opposite trend was seen in the Midlands. Body size, however, also relates to manoeuvrability in the environment, with smaller bodies being more beneficial in more complex environments (Farji-Brener et al., 2004). This may have explained the prevalence of large-bodied ants in the grassland. Although it is difficult to say with certainty how arthropods perceive the complexity of the studied vegetation types, the grassland generally had greater bare ground cover, less leaf litter cover, and less dead wood cover than the wooded biotopes in both regions (Table S6), suggesting that the litter and topsoil layer in grassland may be less structurally complex for the focal organisms. Regarding femur length, several studies suggest ground cover complexity is correlated to femur lengths (Wiescher et al., 2012), with shorter femur lengths being more beneficial in more complex environments. Long legs were observed in the grasslands and short legs in eucalypt compartments in Zululand, corresponding with the expected pattern if the grassland soil surface is perceived as structurally simpler than in plantations. We observed no association between femur length and habitat type in the Midlands.
